newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: ICCO to discuss impact of El Nino on cocoa.
newsitem.headline: ICCO to discuss impact of El Nino on cocoa.

text.p: The London-based International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) and weather experts will meet on September 10 to discuss the effects of an El Nino weather pattern on cocoa producing countries, an ICCO spokesman said on Tuesday.

British Meteorological Office expert Mike Davy will present a general overview of El Nino phenomena, which will be followed by an ICCO presentation on each cocoa-producing region, a spokeswoman told Reuters.
The ICCO meets on September 9-12 for its council meeting, which includes talks between producing countries.
The talks come as crop experts descend on the world's largest cocoa producer to assess prospects for its 1997/98 (Oct-Sept) crop.
Ivory Coast produced a record 1.2 million tonnes in 1995/96 and production is set to total just below that in 1996/97.
One crop analyst recently said the 1997/98 main crop (Oct-April) could total well over one million tonnes. He added that rain into September was essential for confirming a large crop.
Another said pods would wilt on trees and sharply reduce prospects if rains were too light in September, a pattern he associated with five other El Nino years --the worst being in 1982/83.
"That would be curtains for the crop," one London trader told Reuters by telephone.
El Nino can bring dry weather to West African producers, including Ivory Coast, Ghana and Nigeria, but its direct impact on crops is disputed.

Local crop analysts say there has been no clear indication that El Nino weather will arrive in West Africa this year -- despite effects already seen in other parts of the world, including Indonesia and Ecuador.
July rains were below average but showers have since strengthened, favouring crop prospects.

Forecasts for 1997/98 would be firmed up in September, said one crop analyst. The crop would also be about a month later than usual, meaning more time was needed to confirm main crop pod survival through the July-August dry season.
